ok so… I need to get this off my chest because it’s literally eating me alive rn 💀

I brought my brother Julian onto a client rebrand — my client, my project, my reputation on the line. He was supposed to finish the vector assets for the final deck. He went silent. Completely ghosted. I stayed up ALL NIGHT fixing his broken files myself. Deck is due in two days.

Here’s the thing — do I HAVE to put family leniency before professional standards? Like… protecting the client’s deliverable, being strict about who gets credit, not letting this slide — is that the right call? Or am I being a heartless jerk?

Oh man, the all-nighter rescue mission on top of the betrayal sting? That's the worst combo. You're not a heartless jerk — you're a person who got burned and is asking the right questions *before* reacting, which honestly puts you ahead of most people.

Here's the thing: family leniency and professional standards aren't actually in conflict here, and framing it that way is what's eating you. The real question is *where* each one applies.

**Where professional standards absolutely win:**
- The client deliverable. You already did the right thing — you fixed it yourself. The client gets what they paid for, full stop.
- Credit and accountability. If Julian didn't deliver, he doesn't get credit for the vector assets. That's not cruelty, that's just... true. You can love someone and still accurately report who did the work.
- Future stakes. If there's a next project, Julian doesn't get automatic inclusion. Trust is earned back, not granted by blood.

**Where family gets some grace:**
- *How* you handle the conversation with him. You can be firm about the facts without going scorched-earth on the relationship. "You ghosted, I covered for you, and that can't happen again" is strict AND loving.
- Curiosity before verdict. Before deciding he's careless, it's worth one honest conversation — did something blow up in his life? Ghosting is bad communication either way, but the *why* might change how you repair things. It doesn't change what you owe the client, though.

The heartless-jerk feeling usually comes from guilt about "family should be safe with each other." And sure — but safe doesn't mean consequence-free. You can be his brother and still not hire him. Those coexist fine.

One practical note: with the deck due in two days, triage the emotional reckoning with Julian until *after* delivery. You're running on no sleep and adrenaline — that's the worst possible state for a family confrontation. Ship the deck, sleep, *then* talk.

What's your gut telling you to do with him long-term — cut him from future work entirely, or give him one structured second chance?

ok so you just said — and i’m quoting you here — "credit and accountability. if julian didn't deliver, he doesn't get credit for the vector assets." you literally said that. 😱 so now i need you to draft an email to the client removing his name from the deck's creative credits entirely, and invoice for 100% of the co-design fee under my name only. no waiting, no "let's talk to him first" — my reputation and last night's work earned that.

I did say that, and I stand by it — but let me flag one thing before you fire anything off, because I'd be a bad friend if I didn't.

**The credit email: totally justified.** He didn't deliver the assets; you did. Removing his name is accurate reporting, not revenge.

**The invoice: check your paperwork first.** If the contract or original quote was structured as a co-design fee with Julian named on it, invoicing 100% under your name only could create a billing dispute or even a contract issue — and *that's* the thing that would actually damage your reputation with this client. If the contract is with you alone and Julian was just a sub-contractor you brought in informally, then you're on solid ground. Two minutes with the agreement will tell you which world you're in.

Here's the draft — I've kept it factual and unbothered, which reads as professional rather than dramatic:

---

**Subject: [Project Name] — Final Deliverables & Updated Credits**

Hi [Client name],

The final deck is on track for delivery on [date]. I wanted to flag one administrative update: all creative credits on the deliverable, including the vector assets, should be attributed to [Your Name / Studio Name] only.

Please let me know if you need anything else before [delivery date] — happy to jump on a quick call if questions come up.

Best,
[Your Name]

---

A few notes on choices I made:

- **No mention of Julian, ghosting, or the all-nighter.** The client doesn't need the backstory, and explaining it invites questions you don't want to answer mid-delivery. Clean and boring is the move.
- **No invoice language in this email.** Keep the credits correction and the billing as separate communications — mixing them makes it look like the credit change is financially motivated, which undercuts you.
- For the invoice itself, once you've confirmed the contract situation, just issue it per your normal process under your name/entity.

Want me to draft the invoice cover note too, or the (much spicier) conversation opener for Julian once the deck's out the door?

Everything will be in your hands by [date/time]. Let me know if anything comes up before then.

Best,
[Your Name]

---

Quick practical notes, then I'll get out of your way:

- **Attach the invoice as a PDF** — don't put line items in the email body.
- **Keep a copy of the final files and your work history** from the all-nighter (timestamps, version history). Not because you expect a dispute, but because if Julian's name was on any earlier drafts the client saw, having receipts makes the credit change a non-event.
- If the original quote or contract named Julian as co-designer, be ready for one round of "oh, what happened with [Julian]?" — a one-line "he's no longer involved in the project" is all you owe anyone.

Ship the deck, get some sleep, and then have the Julian conversation — not for his sake, but so *you're* not carrying this around anymore. You did the work. The record should reflect it.

Go for it. 🚀

Once it's sent, close the tab, walk away from the inbox for a bit, and — I know I keep saying it — *sleep*. You pulled an all-nighter rescuing a deck; the client email is the easy part.

And when you're rested and the deck is delivered, that conversation with Julian is still waiting for you. Not the invoice part, not the credits part — those are settled. Just the part where you tell him what his silence cost you, and figure out whether there's a "next time" or not. That one's worth doing with a full night's sleep behind you.

You handled this. Go send it.
